answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1863–1947 · industrialist & founder of the Ford Motor Company
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Ford on virtually every quote site, and squarely in keeping with his engineer’s habit of chasing solutions rather than blame — but no primary source pins it. The line is not in My Life and Work (1922), and it is absent from The Henry Ford’s authenticated quotations list, whose staff include only sayings they can trace to a reliable source.

author.name: Henry Ford
author.heading: About Henry Ford
author.bio: Henry Ford (1863–1947) founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903 and, with the moving assembly line and the Model T, brought the automobile within reach of ordinary Americans. A relentless, hands-on problem-solver, he cultivated a public image as a plain-spoken tinkerer — which is exactly why brisk, fix-it aphorisms like this one attach so easily to his name. Many sayings pinned to Ford, however, cannot be traced to anything he actually wrote or said.

cite.sourceCitation: Attributed to Henry Ford; no primary source located. Not found in Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, Page & Co., 1922), nor among the authenticated quotations maintained by The Henry Ford.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Ford
lead: The saying spreads because it sounds like Ford: terse, practical, faintly impatient with anyone who prefers grumbling to fixing. It is the moral of the assembly line boiled down to five words, and that plausibility is precisely what lets an unsourced line ride on a famous name for decades.

The trouble is that plausibility is not provenance. When the institution that guards Ford’s legacy — The Henry Ford — publishes a curated quotations list and notes that anything not on it simply couldn’t be traced to a reliable source, a quote’s absence there is a meaningful signal, not a shrug.
detailsBody: Ford is a magnet for orphaned business aphorisms — ‘whether you think you can or you can’t…’ is the most famous example, itself unverified. A crisp fix-it slogan with no documented parent tends to drift toward the era’s most recognizable fixer, and Ford fits the slot better than almost anyone.

None of this proves Ford never said it in conversation; unrecorded remarks vanish. It means only that, on the documented record available today, the attribution rests on repetition rather than a source.
context.pull: It reads like Ford. That is the whole reason to be careful.
